title: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis Suggested That Neutrophils Predominated the Airways of Children With the Respiratory Syncytial Virus.

analysis.scope_and_question: This review aimed to investigate the predominant cell types in airways inflammation among children with respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) infection, focusing on the role of immune responses in long-term complications.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: The review included a systematic search of PubMed, Embase, Google Scholar, and Web of Science for studies published in English up to 31 August 2025. Bias assessment was conducted using the Joanna Briggs Institute Critical Appraisal Checklist. The meta-analysis was performed on six studies involving 202 RSV-infected children and 97 unaffected controls.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: The meta-analysis found that children with RSV had increased percentages of neutrophils and decreased macrophages in bronchoalveolar lavage fluid. Forest plots showed pooled standard mean differences and 95% confidence intervals for neutrophil and macrophage percentages as 2.12 (1.74 to 2.50) and −3.14 (−4.16 to −2.12), respectively. The review concluded that neutrophils predominated in the airways of children with RSV.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: The review noted that I2 values over 40% indicated heterogeneity among the studies. However, the supplied evidence does not report specific controversies or unresolved mechanisms related to the findings.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: The findings highlight the importance of investigating the role of neutrophils in RSV-induced airway inflammation for future research and clinical practice. The review suggests that further studies are needed to explore the implications of these immune responses on long-term complications.

analysis.summary_en: This systematic review and meta-analysis investigated the predominant cell types in airways inflammation among children with respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) infection. The review focused on the role of immune responses in long-term complications and compared cell types in RSV-infected children with unaffected controls. A meta-analysis of six studies involving 202 RSV-infected children and 97 controls revealed increased neutrophil percentages and decreased macrophage percentages in bronchoalveolar lavage fluid. Forest plots showed pooled standard mean differences and 95% confidence intervals for neutrophil and macrophage percentages as 2.12 (1.74 to 2.50) and −3.14 (−4.16 to −2.12), respectively. The review concluded that neutrophils predominated in the airways of children with RSV. The findings emphasize the need for further research into the implications of these immune responses on long-term health outcomes.

title: Bivalent RSVpreF Effectiveness Against Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV)-Related Respiratory Disease Hospitalization and Emergency Department Visits Across Three RSV Seasons.

analysis.research_question_and_background: Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) protein subunit vaccines reduce the risk of severe outcomes such as hospitalization and emergency department (ED) visits for at least two RSV seasons following vaccination.
analysis.study_design_and_population: This retrospective test-negative case-control study evaluates bivalent RSVpreF VE among adults aged ≥60 years at Kaiser Permanente Southern California, USA, with lower respiratory tract disease (LRTD) or acute respiratory illness (ARI) over three RSV seasons (11/24/2023-4/18/2026).
analysis.methods: Adjusted VE was estimated using odds ratios from multivariable logistic regression or generalized estimating equations.
analysis.main_results: Overall adjusted VE against RSV-related ARI hospitalization/ED visits was 81% (71-87), 64% (48-75), and 60% (15-81), respectively.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: Overall adjusted VE against RSV-related LRTD hospitalization/ED visits was 80% (95% CI 68-87), 70% (95% CI 53-81), and 51% (95% CI -12-78) in the first, second, and third season after vaccination, respectively.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: This suggests bivalent RSVpreF vaccination results in substantial individual and public health benefit.

analysis.summary_en: Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) protein subunit vaccines reduce the risk of severe outcomes such as hospitalization and emergency department (ED) visits for at least two RSV seasons following vaccination. This retrospective test-negative case-control study evaluates bivalent RSVpreF VE among adults aged ≥60 years at Kaiser Permanente Southern California, USA, with lower respiratory tract disease (LRTD) or acute respiratory illness (ARI) over three RSV seasons (11/24/2023-4/18/2026). Adjusted VE was estimated using odds ratios from multivariable logistic regression or generalized estimating equations. Overall adjusted VE against RSV-related ARI hospitalization/ED visits was 81% (71-87), 64% (48-75), and 60% (15-81), respectively. Overall adjusted VE against RSV-related LRTD hospitalization/ED visits was 80% (95% CI 68-87), 70% (95% CI 53-81), and 51% (95% CI -12-78) in the first, second, and third season after vaccination, respectively. This suggests bivalent RSVpreF vaccination results in substantial individual and public health benefit. TRIAL REGISTRATION: ClinicalTrials.gov ID: NCT06077968.

title: Burden of respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) hospitalizations among adults aged 60 years or more in Brazil: A retrospective surveillance database analysis (2013-2024).

analysis.research_question_and_background: Risk increases with advancing age and comorbidities, particularly cardiopulmonary disease and diabetes.
analysis.study_design_and_population: Outcomes included hospitalization frequency, in-hospital mortality, case fatality rates (CFRs), seasonality, healthcare resource utilization, and comorbidities.
analysis.methods: We retrospectively analyzed RSV-associated SARI hospitalizations reported to the national Influenza Epidemiological Surveillance Information System -Gripe.
analysis.main_results: Hospitalization rates increased from 15 per 100,000 in 2024.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: Almost one-third of cases required intensive care unit admission, of whom more than two-thirds needed ventilatory support.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These findings highlight the need to strengthen RSV surveillance and discuss vaccination strategies for adults aged older in Brazil.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: RSV poses a substantial and increasing burden among Brazilian adults aged ≥60 years, with a high CFR, prolonged hospitalizations, and intensive healthcare resource utilization.

analysis.summary_en: Risk increases with advancing age and comorbidities, particularly cardiopulmonary disease and diabetes. Outcomes included hospitalization frequency, in-hospital mortality, case fatality rates (CFRs), seasonality, healthcare resource utilization, and comorbidities. We retrospectively analyzed RSV-associated SARI hospitalizations reported to the national Influenza Epidemiological Surveillance Information System -Gripe. Hospitalization rates increased from 15 per 100,000 in 2024. Almost one-third of cases required intensive care unit admission, of whom more than two-thirds needed ventilatory support. These findings highlight the need to strengthen RSV surveillance and discuss vaccination strategies for adults aged older in Brazil. RSV poses a substantial and increasing burden among Brazilian adults aged ≥60 years, with a high CFR, prolonged hospitalizations, and intensive healthcare resource utilization.

title: Bardoxolone methyl exerts an inhibitory effect on respiratory syncytial virus infection by downregulating IL-6 via the IKKβ/NF-κB signaling pathway.

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to investigate whether bardoxolone methyl (BXM) inhibits respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) infection by modulating the IKKβ/NF-κB/IL-6 axis, addressing the limited therapeutic options for active RSV infection.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study used BEAS-2B cells and BALB/c mice to investigate the effect of BXM on RSV infection, focusing on the modulation of the IKKβ/NF-κB/IL-6 axis.
analysis.methods: BXM was tested in RSV-infected BEAS-2B cells and BALB/c mice, with RT-qPCR, TCID50, plaque reduction assays, Western blotting, and immunofluorescence to assess viral replication and inflammatory mediator expression.
analysis.main_results: BXM significantly suppressed RSV replication and decreased IL-6 expression in vitro and reduced lung viral titers, RSV-F expression, IL-6 expression, IKKβ/NF-κB activation, and RSV-induced lung injury in mice.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings suggest that BXM suppresses RSV replication and inflammation by modulating the IKKβ/NF-κB/IL-6 axis, supporting its potential as a therapeutic candidate for RSV infection.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These results provide experimental evidence supporting BXM as a promising candidate for further development against RSV infection and offer insight into a potential host-targeted therapeutic strategy.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by the use of in vitro and animal models, which may not fully represent human RSV infection. The evidence strength is moderate due to the absence of clinical trial data.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigated the effect of bardoxolone methyl (BXM) on respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) infection in vitro and in mice, demonstrating significant suppression of viral replication and inflammation through modulation of the IKKβ/NF-κB/IL-6 axis, suggesting BXM as a potential therapeutic candidate.

title: Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV)–An Urgent Priority in Respiratory Disease Prevention

analysis.research_question_and_background: Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is a leading cause of lower respiratory tract disease in infants, young children, older adults, and individuals with cardiopulmonary comorbidities or immunocompromised states.
analysis.study_design_and_population: This editorial synthesizes current evidence and policy directions to underscore priority populations and outline actionable levers in financing, procurement, and integrated maternal–child health delivery to accelerate access to RSV prevention.
analysis.methods: Recent advances enable layered prevention through maternal vaccination for infant protection, long-acting monoclonal antibodies for newborns and select toddlers, and vaccines for older adults.
analysis.main_results: This editorial underscores priority populations, synthesizes current evidence and policy directions, and outlines actionable levers in financing, procurement, and integrated maternal–child health delivery to accelerate access, making RSV prevention an urgent and achievable global health priority.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The editorial highlights the potential for RSV prevention to become an urgent and achievable global health priority through targeted interventions and systemic improvements in healthcare delivery.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings inform the need for improved surveillance, equitable access to prevention strategies, and integrated healthcare delivery systems to address RSV-related disease burdens in vulnerable populations.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The supplied evidence does not report specific limitations or evidence gaps related to the study design or implementation of RSV prevention strategies.

analysis.summary_en: This editorial emphasizes the critical role of respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) in causing lower respiratory tract disease across various vulnerable populations, including infants, young children, older adults, and those with cardiopulmonary comorbidities or immunocompromised states. It outlines recent advances in prevention strategies, such as maternal vaccination, monoclonal antibodies, and vaccines for older adults, and highlights the importance of addressing inequities in surveillance, affordability, and delivery to ensure equitable access. The editorial underscores the potential for RSV prevention to become a global health priority through improved financing, procurement, and integrated maternal–child health systems. However, the evidence does not report specific limitations or gaps in the study design or implementation of these strategies. The findings suggest that targeted interventions and systemic improvements in healthcare delivery could significantly enhance RSV prevention efforts, with implications for public health policy and practice.

title: Molecular detection of respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) in hospitalized children at the University Hospital Center of Brazzaville, Republic of the Congo

analysis.research_question_and_background: Epidemiological Respiratory viral infections are among the most common diseases responsible for morbidity and mortality among children in sub-Saharan Africa, with respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) being a major contributor.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The objective of this study was to detect RSV among hospitalized children under five years of age with acute respiratory infections at the University Hospital Center of Brazzaville in the Republic of the Congo.
analysis.methods: Respiratory viruses were identified using rapid antigen detection assays and reverse transcription quantitative polymerase chain reaction (RT-qPCR).
analysis.main_results: Rapid antigen tests detected SARS-CoV-2 in 2 cases (2.5%), whereas RSV and influenza A and B were not detected. In contrast, RT-qPCR identified RSV in 4 samples (4.9%).
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: These findings confirm the circulation of RSV among hospitalized children at the University Hospital Center of Brazzaville and highlight the superior sensitivity of RT-qPCR over rapid antigen tests for RSV detection.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings highlight the importance of using RT-qPCR for accurate RSV detection in clinical settings, which can inform improved diagnostic strategies and targeted interventions for respiratory infections in children.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study was limited to a single hospital and a specific time period, which may affect generalizability. The evidence is moderate due to the limited sample size and the focus on a single geographic location.

analysis.summary_en: This study aimed to detect respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) among hospitalized children under five years of age with acute respiratory infections at the University Hospital Center of Brazzaville in the Republic of the Congo. The researchers used rapid antigen detection assays and reverse transcription quantitative polymerase chain reaction (RT-qPCR) to identify respiratory viruses. While rapid antigen tests did not detect RSV, RT-qPCR identified it in 4 samples (4.9%). These findings confirm the circulation of RSV in the region and emphasize the superior sensitivity of RT-qPCR for RSV detection. The study highlights the need for more accurate diagnostic tools in sub-Saharan Africa to address the burden of respiratory infections in children. However, the study was limited to a single hospital and a specific time period, which may affect the generalizability of the results. The evidence is moderate due to the limited sample size and geographic focus.

title: Post-pandemic re-establishment of respiratory virus seasonality and molecular epidemiology of Rhinovirus/Enterovirus in Northern Italy: a three-year surveillance study (2023-2026).

analysis.research_question_and_background: Following the COVID-19 pandemic, respiratory virus circulation progressively returned towards patterns observed in the pre-pandemic period. However, long-term epidemiological data describing the re-establishment of respiratory viral seasonality and the molecular diversity of Rhinovirus/Enterovirus (RV/EV) remain limited.
analysis.study_design_and_population: To investigate the circulation patterns of respiratory viruses and characterize the RV/EV in Northern Italy, a retrospective observational study was conducted on samples collected between April 2023 and April 2026 at Brescia Civic Hospital.
analysis.methods: Respiratory viruses were detected by real-time PCR, and RV/EV-positive samples were characterized through next-generation sequencing.
analysis.main_results: A total of 6,919 respiratory virus-positive samples were identified. SARS-CoV-2 remained the most frequently detected pathogen, followed by RV/EV, influenza A/B (FLU A/B), adenovirus, respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), parainfluenza virus, bocavirus, and human metapneumovirus. Distinct seasonal peaks were observed for FLU A/B and RSV during winter months, whereas RV/EV circulated continuously throughout the year. Molecular characterization of 224 RV/EV-positive samples revealed substantial genetic diversity. Pediatric patients accounted for the majority of sequenced cases.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: Three years after the end of the COVID-19 pandemic, respiratory viruses have re-established their characteristic seasonal circulation patterns.

analysis.summary_en: This study aimed to investigate the re-establishment of respiratory virus seasonality and molecular diversity of Rhinovirus/Enterovirus (RV/EV) in Northern Italy following the COVID-19 pandemic. Conducted at Brescia Civic Hospital between April 2023 and April 2026, the study used real-time PCR to detect respiratory viruses and next-generation sequencing to characterize RV/EV. A total of 6,919 respiratory virus-positive samples were identified, with SARS-CoV-2 being the most frequently detected pathogen, followed by RV/EV, influenza A/B, adenovirus, RSV, and others. RV/EV showed continuous circulation throughout the year, while FLU A/B and RSV had distinct seasonal peaks during winter. Molecular characterization of 224 RV/EV-positive samples revealed substantial genetic diversity, with pediatric patients accounting for the majority of sequenced cases. The authors concluded that respiratory viruses have re-established their seasonal patterns three years post-pandemic. They emphasized the importance of continuous molecular surveillance for detecting emerging threats. However, they noted that RV/EV remain dominant non-influenza respiratory pathogens with significant genetic heterogeneity, highlighting the need for further research.

title: RESPIRATORY SYNCYTIAL VIRUS INFECTION IN PATIENTS WITH RHEUMATOID ARTHRITIS: DOES DISEASE STATUS AND IMMUNOSUPPRESSION ALTER CLINICAL COURSE, SEVERITY, AND HOSPITALIZATION RISK?

analysis.scope_and_question: This review focuses on respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) infection in patients with rheumatoid arthritis (RA), examining whether disease status and immunosuppression alter clinical course, severity, and hospitalization risk.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: The review is a narrative synthesis of current evidence on RSV epidemiology in immunocompromised populations, pathophysiological mechanisms, risk stratification, clinical presentation, prevention strategies, and management recommendations. It does not report specific databases, search dates, or meta-analysis methods.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: RA patients have substantially higher hospitalization rates for RSV infection (approximately 54%) compared with immunocompetent older adults (6–8%), with frailty being the strongest independent predictor of severe infection (adjusted odds ratio 5.15). Contemporary evidence supports the benefit of RSV vaccination in older adults, though reduced immunogenicity has been documented in patients receiving targeted immunosuppressive therapies.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: The review highlights that the specific burden of RSV disease in RA patients remains incompletely characterized. There is a lack of detailed data on the effectiveness of RSV vaccines in RA patients and the precise mechanisms of increased susceptibility to RSV in this population.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: The review emphasizes the need for individualized risk assessment, optimization of immunosuppression, timely vaccination with enhanced monitoring in high-risk subgroups, early clinical recognition of RSV infection, and evidence-based management approaches.

analysis.summary_en: This review explores the impact of rheumatoid arthritis (RA) and immunosuppression on the clinical course, severity, and hospitalization risk of respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) infection. It synthesizes current evidence on RSV epidemiology, pathophysiology, risk stratification, and management strategies in immunocompromised populations. The findings indicate that RA patients have significantly higher hospitalization rates for RSV compared to immunocompetent individuals, with frailty identified as a key predictor of severe outcomes. While RSV vaccination is beneficial for older adults, reduced immunogenicity in RA patients receiving immunosuppressive therapies is noted. The review underscores the importance of individualized risk assessment, optimized immunosuppression, and targeted vaccination strategies for high-risk subgroups. However, the specific burden of RSV in RA remains incompletely characterized, highlighting the need for further research and improved surveillance.

title: Respiratory Syncytial Virus Vaccine Effectiveness Among US Older Adults, 2023-2024 Season

analysis.research_question_and_background: Importance: Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) causes a substantial number of hospitalizations and deaths among older adults. Two RSV vaccines for individuals aged 60 years or older were approved in 2023; it was important to monitor their clinical effectiveness during routine care in the first RSV season after regulatory approval.
analysis.study_design_and_population: This nationally representative, retrospective cohort study evaluated the effectiveness of RSV vaccines from August 6, 2023, to March 2, 2024. The primary analysis included eligible Medicare fee-for-service beneficiaries aged 65 years or older.
analysis.methods: The study used a retrospective cohort design to estimate vaccine effectiveness by comparing vaccinated and unvaccinated cohorts. Exposures were defined as receipt of RSVPreF3+AS01 or RSVpreF vaccines, and main outcomes were RSV-related hospitalization and RSV-related death.
analysis.main_results: Among 14 819 226 unvaccinated beneficiaries at the beginning of the study, the median age was 74 years (IQR, 70-79 years) and 57.7% were female. By the study end date, 13.9% of beneficiaries had received a RSVPreF3+AS01 vaccine, and 6.4% received a RSVpreF vaccine. Overall estimated vaccine effectiveness compared with the unvaccinated cohort was 81.8% (95% CI, 80.0%-83.4%) against RSV-related hospitalization and 85.0% (95% CI, 75.1%-90.9%) against RSV-related death. Brand-specific vaccine effectiveness against RSV-related hospitalization was 79.9% (95% CI, 77.6%-81.9%) for RSVPreF3+AS01 and 85.1% (95% CI, 82.2%-87.5%) for RSVpreF compared with the unvaccinated cohort.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The study provides clinical evidence of RSV vaccine effectiveness in the first year of vaccine approval. RSV vaccines demonstrated substantial effectiveness within this high-risk older adult population, including among immunocompromised individuals and across all ages 65 years or older.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings inform the clinical effectiveness of RSV vaccines in older adults, which is critical for public health planning and vaccine implementation strategies. This large postmarketing noninterventional study provides valuable data for understanding vaccine impact in the first season after approval.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is a retrospective cohort study, which may be subject to biases and confounding factors. However, the large sample size and nationally representative design provide moderate confidence in the results.

analysis.summary_en: This study evaluates the clinical effectiveness of two RSV vaccines, RSVPreF3+AS01 (GSK) and RSVpreF (Pfizer), among US older adults during the 2023-2024 season. The research is motivated by the significant burden of RSV-related hospitalizations and deaths in this population and the need to monitor vaccine performance post-approval. A nationally representative, retrospective cohort study design was used, analyzing Medicare fee-for-service beneficiaries aged 65 years or older. The study found that overall vaccine effectiveness against RSV-related hospitalization was 81.8% (95% CI, 80.0%-83.4%) and against RSV-related death was 85.0% (95% CI, 75.1%-90.9%). Brand-specific effectiveness was 79.9% (95% CI, 77.6%-81.9%) for RSVPreF3+AS01 and 85.1% (95% CI, 82.2%-87.5%) for RSVpreF. Immunocompromised individuals showed 72.2% (95% CI, 67.4%-76.3%) effectiveness against hospitalization, and effectiveness did not vary significantly with age. The study highlights the substantial effectiveness of RSV vaccines in older adults, including those at higher risk, and provides important postmarketing evidence for vaccine use. However, the retrospective design may introduce biases, limiting the strength of the evidence to moderate.

title: Adjuvanted RSVPreF3 vaccine impact over three respiratory syncytial virus seasons in older adults with comorbidities.

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to evaluate the efficacy of the adjuvanted RSVPreF3 vaccine in older adults with comorbidities during three RSV seasons, addressing the need for targeted prevention strategies in high-risk populations.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study was a multi-country, phase 3 AReSVi-006 trial conducted between May 2021 and May 2024, randomising medically stable ≥60-year-olds in a 1:1 ratio to receive one dose of adjuvanted RSVPreF3 or placebo pre-RSV season.
analysis.methods: Participants were randomised to receive one dose of adjuvanted RSVPreF3 or placebo, and post hoc analyses were conducted to assess vaccine efficacy against RSV-related lower respiratory tract disease, RSV-related acute respiratory illness, and related complications in subgroups with underlying conditions such as COPD, asthma, diabetes, and obesity.
analysis.main_results: Efficacy against RSV-LRTD over three RSV seasons was similar across subgroups with COPD (75.1%, 95% CI: 40.2-91.4), asthma (65.8%, 31.0-84.7), diabetes (69.8%, 37.5-87.1), and obesity (74.1%, 56.4-85.5) as in the overall study population (62.9%, 97.5% CI: 46.7-74.8).
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings suggest that the adjuvanted RSVPreF3 vaccine may be effective in preventing RSV-ARI, RSV-LRTD, and RSV-related complications in medically stable older adults with underlying medical conditions.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The results provide evidence for the potential use of the adjuvanted RSVPreF3 vaccine in preventing RSV-related illnesses in high-risk older adults, which could inform future vaccination strategies for this population.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is based on post hoc analyses, which may introduce bias, and the efficacy against RSV-ARI-related complications showed wide confidence intervals, suggesting moderate evidence strength.

analysis.summary_en: This study evaluated the efficacy of the adjuvanted RSVPreF3 vaccine in older adults with comorbidities during three RSV seasons. The multi-country, phase 3 AReSVi-006 trial randomised medically stable participants aged ≥60 years to receive one dose of the vaccine or placebo. Post hoc analyses showed similar efficacy against RSV-LRTD across subgroups with COPD, asthma, diabetes, and obesity as in the overall population. Efficacy against RSV-ARI was also observed in these subgroups. The study suggests the vaccine may help prevent RSV-ARI, RSV-LRTD, and related complications in high-risk older adults. However, the findings are based on post hoc analyses, which may introduce bias, and the confidence intervals for efficacy against RSV-ARI-related complications were wide, indicating moderate evidence strength.

title: Viral Metagenomic Sequencing Reveals Viral Codetection Patterns in Children with Respiratory Syncytial Virus Infection

analysis.research_question_and_background: Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is a leading cause of pediatric respiratory infections, yet the frequency and composition of viral codetections in affected children have not been extensively profiled using unbiased sequencing approaches.
analysis.study_design_and_population: These findings highlight the polymicrobial complexity of RSV infections and underscore the need for prospective studies to determine which codetections are clinically meaningful.
analysis.methods: Here, we performed viral metagenomic sequencing on nasopharyngeal swabs collected from 42 pediatric patients with confirmed RSV infection to characterize the codetection landscape.
analysis.main_results: Codetections were the rule rather than the exception: 30 of 42 samples harbored at least three viruses, with up to seven distinct viruses detected in a single case.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: Beyond RSV, we identified nine additional human respiratory viruses coexisting across the cohort; several of these fall outside the scope of routine diagnostic panels, although their clinical significance remains uncertain.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: Our results describe the viral codetection landscape in RSV-infected children, revealing a broader spectrum of co-occurring viruses than typically captured by targeted diagnostics, although the clinical significance of most codetections remains uncertain.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: These findings underscore the taxonomic breadth and polymicrobial complexity of respiratory infections in children.

analysis.summary_en: Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is a leading cause of pediatric respiratory infections, yet the frequency and composition of viral codetections in affected children have not been extensively profiled using unbiased sequencing approaches. These findings highlight the polymicrobial complexity of RSV infections and underscore the need for prospective studies to determine which codetections are clinically meaningful. Here, we performed viral metagenomic sequencing on nasopharyngeal swabs collected from 42 pediatric patients with confirmed RSV infection to characterize the codetection landscape. Codetections were the rule rather than the exception: 30 of 42 samples harbored at least three viruses, with up to seven distinct viruses detected in a single case. Beyond RSV, we identified nine additional human respiratory viruses coexisting across the cohort; several of these fall outside the scope of routine diagnostic panels, although their clinical significance remains uncertain. Our results describe the viral codetection landscape in RSV-infected children, revealing a broader spectrum of co-occurring viruses than typically captured by targeted diagnostics, although the clinical significance of most codetections remains uncertain. These findings underscore the taxonomic breadth and polymicrobial complexity of respiratory infections in children.

title: Characteristics and outcomes of adult patients hospitalised with RSV infection, influenza or COVID-19 in Belgium, winter seasons 2023/24 and 2024/25

analysis.research_question_and_background: Severe acute respiratory infections (SARI) cause substantial disease burden in older adults and those with comorbidities. AIM To inform Belgian vaccination policies, we aimed to compare risk profiles and outcomes of influenza, COVID-19 and RSV infections and examine age-related differences.
analysis.study_design_and_population: Adults (≥ 18 years) hospitalised with SARI in nine Belgian sentinel hospitals during the 2023/24 and 2024/25 winter seasons were included. Patients with laboratory-confirmed RSV infection, influenza or COVID-19 were compared in terms of demographics, comorbidities, complications and outcomes.
analysis.methods: Multivariate analyses were applied. Adults 18–64 years were compared with those ≥ 65 years.
analysis.main_results: Among 2,806 patients, 535 (19.1%) had RSV infection, 1,694 (60.4%) influenza and 577 (20.6%) COVID-19. Patients with influenza were significantly younger (mean age 68.9 years) and had significantly fewer comorbidities (89.7%) than patients with RSV (73.8 years; 95.8%) or COVID-19 (74.0 years; 93.6%).
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: Patients with RSV infection had a disease course comparable to patients with influenza or COVID-19 and a higher mortality rate, especially with increasing age.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These findings highlight the importance of RSV vaccination in older adults and those with comorbidities, alongside established vaccination strategies for seasonal influenza and COVID-19.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The supplied evidence does not report specific limitations of the study design or evidence strength assessment.

analysis.summary_en: This study aimed to compare the risk profiles and outcomes of RSV, influenza, and COVID-19 infections in adults hospitalised in Belgium during the winter seasons of 2023/24 and 2024/25. It included 2,806 patients, with 535 having RSV infection, 1,694 influenza, and 577 COVID-19. The study found that patients with RSV were significantly older and had more comorbidities than those with influenza or COVID-19. RSV infection was associated with higher in-hospital mortality compared to both influenza and COVID-19. The results suggest that RSV vaccination should be prioritised for older adults and those with comorbidities, similar to current strategies for influenza and COVID-19. The study used multivariate analyses to compare age-related differences, but it does not report specific limitations or evidence strength assessment.

title: Development and application of nbLIBRA-seq for high-throughput discovery of antigen-specific nanobodies.

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to address the limitations of traditional nanobody discovery methods by developing a high-throughput approach for identifying antigen-specific nanobodies, particularly in the context of respiratory syncytial virus (RSV).
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study involved validating the nbLIBRA-seq method in two different disease settings, focusing on the identification of antigen-specific nanobodies against RSV and other related pathogens.
analysis.methods: The researchers adapted the LIBRA-seq technique to immunized alpacas, using fusion glycoproteins from RSV and human metapneumovirus to screen for antigen-specific heavy-chain antibodies.
analysis.main_results: Over 300 antigen-specific heavy-chain antibodies against human transferrin receptor (TfR1) were identified from a single alpaca blood sample, and 1,125 antigen-specific heavy-chain-expressing B cells were recovered using RSV and human metapneumovirus fusion glycoproteins.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The results demonstrate that nbLIBRA-seq can efficiently identify antigen-specific nanobodies, offering a significant advancement in the development of nanobody-based therapeutics for RSV and related targets.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings suggest that nbLIBRA-seq could enhance the rapid discovery of nanobodies for RSV and other related viruses, potentially accelerating the development of targeted therapeutics and improving public health responses.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited to abstract-level reporting and does not provide detailed statistical analyses or long-term efficacy data, which may affect the strength of the evidence.

analysis.summary_en: This study introduces nbLIBRA-seq, a high-throughput method for identifying antigen-specific nanobodies, with a focus on respiratory syncytial virus (RSV). The researchers validated the technique in two disease settings, demonstrating its ability to rapidly discover nanobodies against RSV and human metapneumovirus. The results highlight the potential of nbLIBRA-seq to improve the development of nanobody-based therapeutics for RSV-related diseases. However, the study is limited to abstract-level reporting and lacks detailed statistical or long-term efficacy data, which may affect the strength of the evidence. The findings could have significant implications for the efficient discovery of nanobodies against RSV and related pathogens, supporting future research and public health applications.

title: Clinical characteristics and outcomes of respiratory syncytial virus and human metapneumovirus ınfections in children under five years of age

analysis.research_question_and_background: This study aimed to compare the clinical characteristics, outcomes, and healthcare costs associated with RSV and hMPV infections in children younger than five years of age.
analysis.study_design_and_population: In this retrospective comparative cohort study, children aged 1–71 months with laboratory-confirmed RSV or hMPV infection identified by multiplex real-time polymerase chain reaction were included. RSV cases identified between September 2022 and April 2023 and hMPV cases identified between September 2022 and December 2025 were included. Both outpatient and hospitalized patients evaluated at a tertiary pediatric hospital were enrolled.
analysis.methods: The study used multiplex real-time polymerase chain reaction to identify laboratory-confirmed RSV and hMPV infections in children aged 1–71 months. Data were collected from a tertiary pediatric hospital and analyzed for clinical characteristics, outcomes, and healthcare costs.
analysis.main_results: Bronchiolitis, cough, nasal congestion, tachypnea, chest retractions, rhonchi, oxygen supplementation, inhaled therapies, corticosteroid use, and hospitalization were more common among children with RSV infection (all p < 0.05).
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: This large pediatric cohort showed that RSV predominantly affected younger children and was associated with more bronchiolitis, hospitalization, and supportive treatment needs, whereas hMPV was more common in older children with comorbidities and was more frequently associated with pneumonia.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings can inform targeted surveillance and management strategies for RSV infections in younger children, particularly in settings where hospitalization and supportive care are required.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited to a single tertiary pediatric center in Türkiye, which may affect the generalizability of the results. The evidence is moderate due to the observational nature of the study and potential geographic bias.

analysis.summary_en: This study compares the clinical characteristics and outcomes of respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) and human metapneumovirus (hMPV) infections in children under five years of age. It is a retrospective comparative cohort study conducted at a tertiary pediatric hospital in Türkiye, including cases from September 2022 to December 2025. The study found that RSV infections were more common in younger children and associated with more severe symptoms such as bronchiolitis, hospitalization, and the need for supportive treatments, while hMPV was more frequently linked to pneumonia in older children with comorbidities. The results suggest that RSV and hMPV have distinct clinical impacts in this age group, which could inform targeted surveillance and management strategies. However, the study's findings may be limited by its focus on a single geographic location, which could affect generalizability. The evidence is considered moderate due to the observational design and potential for geographic bias.

title: Human metapneumovirus in central China, 2024–2025: epidemiology, co-infections, and temporal dynamics

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to address the limited data on HMPV epidemiology in the post-pandemic period and to understand its co-infection patterns for improved surveillance and prevention.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A retrospective analysis of 36,143 respiratory specimens from ILI/SARI patients in Henan, China, was conducted between 2024 and 2025.
analysis.methods: Multiplex PCR was used to detect HMPV and 14 other pathogens. Positivity rates, enrichment ratios, co-infection patterns, pathogen associations (OR/PR), and temporal dynamics (cross-correlation and regression) were assessed.
analysis.main_results: Overall HMPV positivity was 3.96% (1,432/36,143), with a sharp inter-year difference: 7.1% in 2024 vs. 1.7% in 2025, peaking at 26.2% during week 48. Children aged 3–5 years had the highest positivity (8.6%; enrichment ratio 2.18).
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The study highlights the high rates of bacterial co-infections with HMPV and the significant association with RSV at a 1-week lag, indicating potential interactions between these pathogens.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings suggest the importance of integrated surveillance for HMPV and RSV, as well as age-targeted prevention strategies, particularly for children aged 3–5 years.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited to a single geographic region and relies on sentinel surveillance data, which may not be fully representative. The evidence is moderate due to these constraints.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigated the epidemiology of human metapneumovirus (HMPV) in Henan, China, during 2024–2025, focusing on its co-infection patterns and temporal dynamics. The research aimed to fill knowledge gaps regarding HMPV's role in respiratory infections post-pandemic. Using multiplex PCR, the study analyzed 36,143 respiratory specimens from ILI/SARI patients, revealing an overall positivity rate of 3.96% with a notable inter-year variation. Children aged 3–5 years showed the highest HMPV positivity, and co-infections were common, particularly with Streptococcus pneumoniae and Haemophilus influenzae. HMPV was positively associated with HBoV and RSV at a 1-week lag, but negatively associated with influenza virus and RSV. These findings emphasize the need for integrated surveillance and age-specific prevention strategies, though the study's geographic limitation and reliance on sentinel data suggest moderate evidence strength.

title: Trends and estimated costs of hospitalizations potentially associated with respiratory syncytial virus among children in Brazil, 2014-2025

analysis.research_question_and_background: ABSTRACTBackground: Respiratory syncytial virus, a major cause of respiratory infections and hospitalizations in young children, especially bronchiolitis, is an important burden to the health system in Brazil.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A simple linear regression model (lm function) was applied to assess the association between average length of stay (independent variable) and adjusted average cost per hospitalization (dependent variable), corrected for inflation and converted to international dollars (Int$) using the purchasing power parity (PPP) conversion factor of 2.524 BRL/Int$, as recommended by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development and the World Bank 22 , 23 .
analysis.methods: Scatter plots were generated for each region, with trend lines based on the fitted regression model using geom_point function to plot the scatter points and geom_smooth (method = “lm”) from ggplot2 14 to add the regression line.
analysis.main_results: The north showed a weaker pattern (0.52) (Supplementary Figure 2).Regional boxplots exhibited a consistent seasonality, with hospitalization peaks between March and June.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: Data were exported as .csv files and processed using R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Viena, Áustria, for organization, cleaning, and aggregation to support the statistical and temporal analyses 9 , 10 .
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: In the northeast, correlation was lower (r = 0.50; p < 0.001), with a daily increase of Int$ 51.70, similar to the national trend but with less impact.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The north had the weakest correlation (r = 0.47; p < 0.001; R2 = 22.5%), although significant, with an additional Int$ 33.63 per additional day (Supplementary Figure 3; Table 2).

analysis.summary_en: ABSTRACTBackground: Respiratory syncytial virus, a major cause of respiratory infections and hospitalizations in young children, especially bronchiolitis, is an important burden to the health system in Brazil. A simple linear regression model (lm function) was applied to assess the association between average length of stay (independent variable) and adjusted average cost per hospitalization (dependent variable), corrected for inflation and converted to international dollars (Int$) using the purchasing power parity (PPP) conversion factor of 2.524 BRL/Int$, as recommended by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development and the World Bank 22 , 23 . Scatter plots were generated for each region, with trend lines based on the fitted regression model using geom_point function to plot the scatter points and geom_smooth (method = “lm”) from ggplot2 14 to add the regression line. The north showed a weaker pattern (0.52) (Supplementary Figure 2).Regional boxplots exhibited a consistent seasonality, with hospitalization peaks between March and June. Data were exported as .csv files and processed using R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Viena, Áustria, for organization, cleaning, and aggregation to support the statistical and temporal analyses 9 , 10 . In the northeast, correlation was lower (r = 0.50; p < 0.001), with a daily increase of Int$ 51.70, similar to the national trend but with less impact. The north had the weakest correlation (r = 0.47; p < 0.001; R2 = 22.5%), although significant, with an additional Int$ 33.63 per additional day (Supplementary Figure 3; Table 2).

title: Airborne Virus Shedding of Respiratory Syncytial Virus Compared to Influenza A Virus in Hospitalized Patients

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to assess the potential for airborne shedding of influenza A virus (IAV) and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) in hospitalized patients, addressing the importance of airborne transmission for respiratory viruses.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study compared the presence of viral RNA in air samples collected from 59 hospitalized patients, 39 with IAV infection and 21 with RSV infection, including one co-infected patient.
analysis.methods: Air sampling was performed using a vacuum cleaner with a detachable soluble air filter, collecting samples 50 cm from the patient's face for 2 minutes, and analyzed for viral RNA by RT-qPCR.
analysis.main_results: Air samples were more frequently positive in RSV-infected patients (57%) compared to IAV-infected patients (15%), with a p-value of 0.0012. Multivariable analysis confirmed RSV infections were associated with higher rates of air sample positivity after adjusting for nasopharyngeal viral load.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings suggest different aerosol shedding between RSV and IAV, although the infectious potential of these differences remains to be determined.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These results could inform surveillance and infection control strategies, particularly in the context of RSV, which showed higher aerosol shedding potential.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study's design limitations, such as the small sample size and the absence of direct clinical outcomes, limit the generalizability of the findings. The evidence strength is moderate.

analysis.summary_en: This study compared the airborne shedding of influenza A virus and respiratory syncytial virus in hospitalized patients, finding that RSV had a higher rate of air sample positivity, suggesting different aerosol shedding patterns between the two viruses.

title: Computational designing of multiepitope based vaccine (MEBV) candidate against human metapneumovirus (HMPV) using immunoinformatics approach

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to design a multiepitope vaccine candidate against human metapneumovirus (HMPV) due to its role as a respiratory pathogen closely related to respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), which lacks an available vaccine.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study involved computational designing of a multiepitope vaccine (MEBV) candidate against HMPV, using immunoinformatics methods to identify potential epitopes and assess vaccine properties.
analysis.methods: The researchers used computational tools to screen three viral proteins for epitopes, combined them with linkers and beta-defensin as an adjuvant, and performed molecular docking and MD simulations to evaluate interactions with human TLR3.
analysis.main_results: The MEBV candidate was composed of 13 MHC-I epitopes, one MHC-II epitope, and four linear B-cell epitopes, resulting in a 296-amino-acid construct with an antigenicity score of 0.6644. Molecular docking and MD simulations showed a high degree of interaction with human TLR3 with binding energy of −14.6.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings suggest that the proposed MEBV has potential as an immunogen for HMPV, offering a novel approach to vaccine development against this virus.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The results provide a foundation for further research into HMPV vaccine development, which could improve surveillance, diagnosis, and prevention strategies for HMPV-related respiratory infections.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is based on computational methods and does not include experimental validation, which limits the strength of the evidence to moderate.

analysis.summary_en: This study presents a computational approach to designing a multiepitope vaccine (MEBV) candidate against human metapneumovirus (HMPV), a respiratory pathogen closely related to RSV. The researchers identified three viral proteins with no similarity to the host genome and selected epitopes for MHC-I, MHC-II, and B-cell recognition. The MEBV construct, containing 13 MHC-I epitopes, one MHC-II epitope, and four linear B-cell epitopes, was evaluated for antigenicity and interaction with human TLR3, showing a binding energy of −14.6. The findings suggest the MEBV has potential as an immunogen for HMPV, offering a novel vaccine design strategy. However, the study is limited to computational methods without experimental validation, resulting in moderate evidence strength.

title: Retrospective analysis of multiplex panel tests in the diagnosis of respiratory tract infections

analysis.research_question_and_background: Respiratory tract infections (RTIs) remain a major global health concern, particularly in children.
analysis.study_design_and_population: This retrospective single-center study investigated the epidemiology of respiratory pathogens detected by mPCR, focusing on their distribution, age-related patterns, seasonal variation, and coinfections.
analysis.methods: Nasopharyngeal swab samples from 328 patients with suspected acute RTIs, collected between January 2022 and December 2023, were analyzed using the BioFire FilmArray Respiratory Panel 2.1.
analysis.main_results: At least one respiratory pathogen was detected in 270 of 328 specimens, yielding an overall positivity rate of 82.3%. Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) was the third most frequently identified agent, with a prevalence of 14.2%.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The study highlights the significant role of RSV in RTIs and demonstrates the utility of mPCR in identifying viral pathogens efficiently.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These findings support the role of mPCR in improving diagnostic accuracy and providing valuable regional epidemiological data for RSV.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited to a single-center retrospective analysis, which may affect generalizability, and the evidence is based on abstract-only data, resulting in a moderate confidence assessment.

analysis.summary_en: This study aimed to evaluate the epidemiology of respiratory pathogens, with a focus on respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), using multiplex PCR (mPCR) in a single-center retrospective analysis. The research highlights the importance of RSV in respiratory tract infections, particularly in children, and demonstrates the diagnostic value of mPCR in identifying viral agents. The study found that RSV was the third most common pathogen, with a prevalence of 14.2%, and that coinfections were common, especially involving adenovirus and HRV/HEV. The results indicate a seasonal trend with higher positivity rates in winter and spring. The findings suggest that mPCR can enhance diagnostic accuracy and provide useful epidemiological insights for RSV. However, the study's limitations include its single-center design and reliance on abstract-only data, which may affect the strength of the conclusions.

title: RSV Vaccination in Systemic Autoimmune Rheumatic Diseases: A Systematic Review.

analysis.scope_and_question: Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) vaccination is available for older adults. The review focuses on the vaccination of patients with systemic autoimmune rheumatic diseases (SARDs), including those receiving immunosuppressive therapies, which were excluded from trials.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: A systematic review was conducted evaluating RSV epidemiology, vaccine effectiveness, immunogenicity, and safety in adults with SARDs. Databases were searched from inception to 28th January 2026, and 49 studies were included in the analysis, including observational studies, clinical trials, and pharmacovigilance reports.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: Only one study reported RSV outcomes in SARD patients. RSV vaccines demonstrated first-season effectiveness of 60–73% in immunocompromised adults, with evidence of attenuated and more rapidly waning protection compared with immunocompetent populations. Observational data suggest autoimmune and immunocompromising conditions are associated with increased RSV-associated hospitalisation, although attribution is uncertain due to bias and data limitations. No consistent autoimmune safety signals were identified, though data in SARD populations remain limited.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: No study evaluated vaccine effectiveness stratified by DMARD-class. The absence of DMARD-specific data represents an evidence gap. Heterogeneity in study designs and limited data on safety and efficacy in SARD patients are noted.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: Vaccination appears effective and safe in immunocompromised populations, but protection may wane more rapidly. Until further evidence emerges, vaccination should be considered for eligible patients using a personalised framework.

analysis.summary_en: A systematic review of RSV vaccination in patients with systemic autoimmune rheumatic diseases (SARDs) found limited evidence. RSV vaccines showed 60-73% effectiveness in immunocompromised adults, but protection wanes more rapidly. Observational data suggest increased RSV hospitalisation in SARD patients, though attribution is uncertain. DMARD-specific data are lacking, and further research is needed.

title: Maternal RSV vaccination: clinical efficacy, safety, and global policy considerations: a systematic review.

analysis.scope_and_question: ABSTRACT Background Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is among the leading causes of lower respiratory tract illness in newborns worldwide.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: Methods PROSPERO registered this PRISMA-compliant systematic review (CRD42024566335).
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: Results Sixteen publications – four real-world studies and twelve generated from nine separate parent trials/datasets (including three subgroup or subset analyses and post-hoc studies from two RCTs) – met the inclusion criteria.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: This study reviews evidence on the efficacy and safety of maternal RSV vaccination.

analysis.summary_en: This systematic review examines the efficacy and safety of maternal RSV vaccination, finding that it reduces severe RSV-related lower respiratory tract infections in newborns with varying efficacy rates. While post-vaccination responses are generally mild, there are concerns about preterm birth risks that vary by vaccine formulation.
